title: David Returns to a Divided Kingdom
overview: After his son Absalom dies in a failed revolt, David grieves, is pushed back into leading, and returns to Jerusalem amid old grudges, mercy, loyalty and tribal rivalry.

parts.label: Grief and a blunt warning (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: David's loud mourning for Absalom, the son who had tried to overthrow him, made his loyal soldiers feel their victory was shameful. Joab warned that the army would leave him by nightfall unless he thanked them, so David went and sat at the city gate, the public place where a king met his people.

parts.label: Bringing the king back (vv. 9-15)
parts.note: The revolt had split the nation, and the tribes argued over why no one had invited David home. David waited to be asked rather than marching back by force, and he won over his own tribe of Judah by promising Amasa, who had led Absalom's army, Joab's job.

parts.label: Mercy for Shimei (vv. 16-23)
parts.note: Shimei, a man from the family of the earlier king Saul, had cursed David and thrown stones at him as he fled. Now he arrived with a thousand men and begged forgiveness, and David refused Abishai's call to kill him, saying a day of restored kingship was no day for executions.

parts.label: Mephibosheth and Ziba (vv. 24-30)
parts.note: Saul's grandson Mephibosheth had gone unwashed and unshaven as a sign of mourning, and he said his servant Ziba had tricked him and lied about him. David, apparently unsure who was telling the truth, split the land between them, a ruling many readers have found unfair.

parts.label: Barzillai's farewell (vv. 31-39)
parts.note: Barzillai, a wealthy old man from east of the Jordan, had fed David's camp during the war. He turned down a life at court because he wanted to die near his parents' graves, and he sent a younger man, likely his son, in his place.

parts.label: Judah and Israel quarrel (vv. 40-43)
parts.note: The northern tribes claimed ten shares in the king because they were ten tribes, while Judah claimed him as close family. This bitter rivalry leads straight into a new revolt in the next chapter and hints at the kingdom's later split into two.

think: Have you ever had to put your own grief aside because other people were depending on you, and do you think that was fair to ask?
